Course title:
Flood Insurance Basics

Learning objectives:
  1. Describe the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), identify the types of buildings and other property that can get coverage under this program, and identify who needs flood insurance
  2. Explain the function of flood maps and flood zones under the NFIP
  3. Discuss the types of policies under the NFIP, including dwelling policies, general property policies, and residential condominium policies, and explain their uses
  4. Explain the general rules governing policies, including deductibles, waiting periods, cancellations, etc
  5. Describe the rating steps that must be followed to set a premium for an NFIP policy
  6. Discuss the way in which claims are handled, including responsibilities of the insured; and
  7. Describe an agent’s responsibilities is selling NFIP insurance to consumers

Raw course content (up to 8000 words from source document — paraphrase themes; do not quote at length):
Flood Insurance Basics (Course ID: 529) Table of Contents 1.0 Anywhere There Is Water 1 2.0 The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) Background 2 2.1 Community Participation 2 2.2 Eligible Buildings 3 2.3 Ineligible Property 3 2.4 Ineligible Risks 3 2.5 Coastal Barrier Resources System and Other Protected Areas 4 2.6 Who Needs Flood Insurance? 4 3.0 Flood Maps and Zone Determinations 5 3.1 Types of Flood Maps 5 3.2 Changing or Correcting a Flood Map 6 4.0 Policies and Products Available 7 4.1 Dwelling Policy 7 4.2 General Property Policy 7 4.3 Residential Condominium Building Association Policy (RCBAP) 8 4.4 Preferred Risk Policy (PRP) 8 4.5 Flood Policy Definitions 9 4.6 Flood Policy Coverages 13 4.7 Property Not Covered 13 4.8 Exclusions 14 5.0 NFIP General Rules 17 5.1 Deductibles 17 5.2 Loss Settlement 18 5.2.1 Coinsurance Penalty in RCBAP 20 5.3 Reduction and Reformation of Coverage 21 5.4 Waiting Period 22 5.5 Policy Term 22 5.6 Cancellations 24 6.0 Rating 29 6.1 Rating Steps 29 7.0 Claims Handling Process 30 7.1 Insured's Responsibilities 30 7.2 Appealing a Claim 31 7.3 Limitations On Appeals 31 7.4 Appeals Resolution 31 7.5 Producer's Responsibilities 31 8.0 Agent Responsibility 32 8.1 Agent Resources 33 10.0 Conclusion 33 1.0 Anywhere There Is Water Flooding can occur anywhere there is water. Flooding is defined as: A general and temporary condition of partial or complete inundation of two or more acres of normally dry land area or of two or more properties (at least one of which is the policyholder’s property) from: overflow of inland or tidal waters; unusual and rapid accumulation or runoff of surface waters from any source; or – mudflow; or collapse or subsidence of land along the shore of a lake or similar body of water as a result of erosion or undermining caused by waves or currents of water exceeding anticipated cyclical levels that result in a flood. The most common events that result in flooding include hurricanes, broken levees, outdated or clogged drainage systems, or a heavy rainfall. Risk of flooding is based on a number of factors, including: history, rainfall, river-flow and tidal surge data, topography, flood-control measures, and changes due to building and development. Unfortunately, it takes little water to do major damage and a typical homeowners policy does not include coverage for flooding, making flood insurance a necessity for those at increased risk for flooding. Congress requires that federally regulated or insured lenders require flood insurance on properties that are located in areas at high risk of flooding. High risk areas have a 1% or greater chance of flooding in any given year, which is equivalent to a 26% chance of flooding during a 30-year mortgage. Although homes and businesses located in moderate-to-low risk areas are typically not required to have flood insurance, it is highly recommended because they too can be financially vulnerable to floods. This course will discuss the National Flood Insurance Program and the coverage options available to address potential flood hazards. Learning Objectives After you have completed this course, you will be able to . . . Describe the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), identify the types of buildings and other property that can get coverage under this program, and identify who needs flood insurance; Explain the function of flood maps and flood zones under the NFIP; Discuss the types of policies under the NFIP, including dwelling policies, general property policies, and residential condominium policies, and explain their uses; Explain the general rules governing policies, including deductibles, waiting periods, cancellations, etc.; Describe the rating steps that must be followed to set a premium for an NFIP policy; Discuss the way in which claims are handled, including responsibilities of the insured; and Describe an agent’s responsibilities is selling NFIP insurance to consumers. The NFIP is administered by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the information contained in this course relies heavily on the FEMA Flood Insurance Manual. FEMA updates this manual a couple times a year; you can access the current and past manuals here. 2.0 The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) Background In 1968, Congress established the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) to: Authorize a flood insurance program that, over time, could be made available on a nationwide basis through the cooperative effort of the federal government and the private insurance industry. Provide flexibility in the program so that such flood insurance would be based on workable methods of pooling risks, minimizing costs and distributing burdens equitably among the general public and those who would be protected by flood insurance. Encourage state and local governments to use wisely the lands under their jurisdictions by considering the hazards of flood when rendering decisions on the future use of such land in order to minimize damage. In 1983, the Write Your Own (WYO) Program was established through a joint effort of FEMA and the private insurance industry. According to FEMA: The WYO Program allows participating property and casualty insurance companies to write and service the Standard Flood Insurance Policy in their own names. The companies receive an expense allowance for policies written and claims processed while the Federal Government retains responsibility for underwriting losses. The WYO Program operates as part of the NFIP, and is subject to its rules and regulations. 2.1 Community Participation Under the NFIP program, communities agree, through adoption of codes and ordinances, to regulate the use of flood-prone land. In exchange, FEMA makes flood insurance coverage available on buildings and their contents throughout the community. To assist communities with identifying these flood-prone areas, FEMA has created flood hazard maps. In addition to assisting communities, the flood hazard maps assist insurance producers in setting rates and lenders with regard to purchase requirements. 2.2 Eligible Buildings Flood insurance policies are available only for structures "with two or more outside rigid walls and a fully secured roof that is affixed to a permanent site" and must resist: flotation, collapse, and lateral movement. Additionally, at least 51 percent of the actual cash value of buildings, together with any machinery and equipment that are a part of the buildings, must be above ground level. The exception to this 51 percent rule is if the lowest level is at or above the BFE and is below ground because the earth is used as insulation material through energy-efficient building techniques. 2.3 Ineligible Property Buildings in violation of state or local floodplain management laws, regulations or ordinances may not be eligible for coverage. Additionally, contents and personal property located in these buildings are not eligible for coverage. Key Point: Section 1316 of the NFIA allows states to declare a structure in violation of a law, regulation, or ordinance and flood insurance is not available for properties placed on a "1316 Property List." Insurance will once again be available if the condition creating the violation is fixed and the 1316 Declaration withdrawn. 2.4 Ineligible Risks In addition to ineligible buildings, there are ineligible risks associated with the program. These include: Boat Repair Dock Boat Storage Over Water Boathouses Camper Cooperative Unit Within Cooperative Building Decks (except for steps and landing; maximum landing area of 16 sq. ft.) Drive-In Bank Teller Unit (located outside walls of building) Fuel Pump Gazebo (unless it qualifies as a building) Greenhouse (unless it has at least two rigid walls and a roof) Hot tub or spa (unless it is installed as a bathroom fixture) Open Stadium Pavilion (unless it qualifies as a building) Pole Barn (unless it qualifies as a building) Pumping Station (unless it qualifies as a building) Storage Tank--Gasoline, Water, Chemicals, Sugar, etc. Swimming Pool Bubble Swimming Pool (indoor or outdoor) Tennis Bubble Tent Time Sharing Unit Within Multi-Unit Building Travel Trailer (unless converted to a permanent onsite building meeting the community's floodplain management permit requirements) Water Treatment Plant (unless 51 percent of its actual cash value is above ground) 2.5 Coastal Barrier Resources System and Other Protected Areas The Coastal Barrier Resources Act (CBRA), and the Coastal Barrier Improvement Act (CBIA) of 1990, were implemented to: minimize loss of life by discouraging development in high-risk areas, reduce wasteful expenditures of federal resources, and preserve the ecological integrity of areas Congress designates as a Coastal Barrier Resources System (CBRS) and Otherwise Protected Areas (OPAs), by prohibiting federal expenditures or financial assistance (including flood insurance) for residential or commercial development in areas identified as high risk. FEMA provides a list of communities where coastal barriers or OPAs are identified and should be consulted prior to insuring a property. You may view the complete list in the Flood Insurance Manual. 2.6 Who Needs Flood Insurance? The Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973 identifies the following (if they are located in identified areas of special flood hazards) as being required to purchase flood insurance if they wish to receive any type of federal assistance (e.g., any loan, grant, guaranty, insurance, payment, subsidy or disaster assistance): individuals, businesses, and others buying, building, or improving property. Aside from this requirement most forms of disaster assistance requires a Presidential declaration, which does not occur in all flooding incidents. Most disaster assistance is in the form of a loan, which must be paid back with interest. The duration of a Small Business Administration (SBA) disaster home loan could extend to 30 years. Knowledge Check To be eligible for NFIP flood insurance, a building must resist all the following EXCEPT: (Refer to Section 2.2, page 3) Collapse [Your answer is incorrect. A building must resist collapse, but need not resist wetness.] Flotation [Your answer is incorrect. A building must resist floatation, but need not resist wetness.] Lateral movement [Your answer is incorrect. A building must resist lateral movement, but need not resist wetness.] Wetness [Your answer is correct. A building need not resist wetness.] Which of the following structures would be eligible for flood insurance? (Refer to Section 2.4, page 3) Boat repair dock [Your answer is incorrect. A two-story house is eligible for flood insurance. A boat repair dock is not.] Drive-in bank teller unit (separate from the bank building) [Your answer is incorrect. A two-story house is eligible for flood insurance. A drive-in bank teller unit (separate from the bank building) dock is not.] Two-story house [Your answer is correct. A two-story house is eligible for flood insurance.] Swimming pool [Your answer is incorrect. A two-story house is eligible for flood insurance. A swimming pool is not.] 3.0 Flood Maps and Zone Determinations FEMA provides all participating communities with copies of community flood maps. Copies of the maps are also kept with the planning or building departments of the community for review. Information about flood maps can be obtained from the FEMA Map Service Center website. 3.1 Types of Flood Maps There are two types of maps used for rating flood insurance: the Flood Hazard Boundary Map (FHBM) and the Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM). The FHBM is issued by FEMA and represents the official map of a community, showing where the boundaries of the flood, mudflow, and related erosion areas having special hazards have been designated. A FIRM is the official map of a community on which FEMA has delineated the special hazard areas and the risk premium zones applicable to the community. The FIRM is typically used for Regular Program communities. Key Point: An FHBM is the initial flood hazard identification map, typically used in Emergency Program communities. There are times when Regular Program communities will use a map that was originally published as an FHBM. When this occurs, a letter accompanies the map outlining conversion to the Regular Program and indicating that the FHBM map should now be considered a FIRM. 3.2 Changing or Correcting a Flood Map There are times when a change to a flood map is required and the NFIP has certain procedures that must be followed to facilitate such amendments. The Flood Manual outlines these procedures as: Letter of Map Amendment (LOMA). A LOMA is used in instances where an applicant/insured believes they are being required to purchase flood insurance in error and that their property is not actually located in the SFHA. The insured then requests a LOMA asking FEMA to make a correction. Letter of Map Revision (LOMR). A LOMR is an official revision to a current FEMA map. A LOMR must be requested directly from the CEO of a community, as any changes made because of the LOMR must be adopted by the community. Physical Map Revision. A physical map revision is exactly what it sounds like: change and republication of an existing map to change flood insurance zones, floodplain delineations, flood elevations, floodways, and planimetric features. Knowledge Check Which of the following maps are typically used for Regular Program Communities? (Refer to Section 3.1, page 6) Flood Hazard Boundary Map (FHBM) [Your answer is incorrect. A FIRM is typically used for Regular Program communities. A FHBM is typically used in the Emergency Program.] Special Flood Hazard Map (SFHM) [Your answer is incorrect. A FIRM is typically used for Regular Program communities. A SFHM is not a real map type.] Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) [Your answer is correct. A FIRM is the official map of a community on which FEMA has delineated the special hazard areas and the risk premium zones applicable to the community. The FIRM is typically used for Regular Program communities.] US Geological Survey (USGS) [Your answer is incorrect. A FIRM is typically used for Regular Program communities. USGS is not a flood map type.] 4.0 Policies and Products Available 4.1 Dwelling Policy The Dwelling Policy is available only for buildings and/or residential contents on a single- or two-to four- family dwelling. In the Regular and Emergency Programs, the Dwelling Policy provides a building and/or contents coverage for: Detached, single-family, non-condominium residence with incidental occupancy limited to less than 50 percent of the total floor area; Two- to four-family, non-condominium building with incidental occupancy limited to less than 25 percent of the total floor area; Dwelling unit in residential condominium building; Residential townhouse/row house; Personal contents in a non-residential building. 4.2 General Property Policy The General Property Policy is available for a building and/or contents on other residential or non-residential buildings. In the Regular and Emergency Programs, this includes: Hotel or motel with normal guest occupancy of less than six months; Licensed bed-and-breakfast inn; Retail shop, restaurant, or other business; Mercantile building; Grain bin, silo, or other farm building; Agricultural or industrial processing facility; Factory; Warehouse; Pool house, clubhouse, or other recreational building; House of worship; School; Nursing home; Non-residential condominium; Condominium building with less than 75% of its total floor area in residential use; Detached garage; Tool shed; Stock, inventory, or other commercial contents. 4.3 Residential Condominium Building Association Policy (RCBAP) The Residential Condominium Building Association Policy (RCBAP) insures a residential condominium building and all units within the building. The caveat is that the building must be located in a Regular Program community and at least 75 percent of the total floor area, residential. Responsibility for insurance is split between the condominium association and unit owners. The association is responsible for insuring the building and common areas (similar to the responsibility of a landlord) using the RCBAP and unit owners can insure their units and contents using the Dwelling form. 4.4 Preferred Risk Policy (PRP) We are going to briefly mention a policy type that was recently eliminated. It was the Preferred Risk Policy (PRP), which offered low-cost coverage to owners and tenants of properties located in zones B, C, and X in eligible Regular Program communities. Although this form was eliminated as a separate policy-type as of October 1, 2021, the low-cost coverage offered under the form was incorporated into the Dwelling Policy. Key Point: For residential properties, the maximum coverage combination is $250,000: building and $100,000 contents. Up to $100,000 contents-only coverage is available. For non-residential properties, the maximum coverage combination is $500,000 building and $500,000 contents. Up to $500,000 contents-only coverage is available. Only one building can be insured per policy, and only one policy can be written on each building. Coverage previously available under the PRP that may be gotten now under the Dwelling Policy includes: Combined building/contents insurance, available for owners of all eligible occupancy types—one- to four-family properties (including individual condominium units in condominium buildings), other residential properties, and non-residential properties. Contents-only coverage, available for tenants and owners of all eligible occupancies, unless the contents are located entirely in a basement. Eligibility for the PRP was also based on a building’s flood loss history, meaning if one of the following conditions existed within any 10-year period (regardless of any change(s) in ownership of the building), the building was not eligible for the PRP: Two flood insurance claim payments, each more than $1,000; or Three or more flood insurance claim payments, regardless of amount; or Two federal flood disaster relief payments (including loans and grants), each more than $1,000; or Three federal flood disaster relief payments (including loans and grants), regardless of amount; or One flood insurance claim payment and one federal flood disaster relief payment (including loans and grants), each more than $1,000. These factors are now taken into account in the Dwelling Policy in determining the policyholder’s premium rate. 4.5 Flood Policy Definitions Act. The National Flood Insurance Act of 1968 and any amendments to it. Actual Cash Value (ACV). The cost to replace an insured item of property at the time of loss, less the value of its physical depreciation. Application. The statement made and signed by the customer or agent in applying for the policy. The application provides information used to determine the eligibility of the risk, the kind of policy to be issued, and the correct premium payment. The application is part of the flood insurance policy. The correct premium payment must accompany the application. Base Flood. A flood having a one percent chance of being equaled or exceeded in any given year. Basement. Any area of the building, including any sunken room or sunken portion of a room, having its floor below ground level (subgrade) on all sides. Binder or Certificate of Insurance. A temporary agreement between company, producer, and insured that the policy is in effect. The NFIP does not recognize binders. However, the NFIP recognizes Certificates of Insurance for renewal policies. Blanket Insurance. A single amount of insurance applying to more than one building and/or contents. Blanket insurance is not permitted under the NFIP. Building. A building is defined in the program as: A structure with two or more outside rigid walls and a fully secured roof, that is affixed to a permanent site; A manufactured home (a "manufactured home," also known as a mobile home, is a structure: built on a permanent chassis, transported to its site in one or more sections, and affixed to a permanent foundation); or A travel trailer without wheels, built on a chassis and affixed to a permanent foundation, that is regulated under the community's floodplain management and building ordinances or laws. This definition does not include a gas or liquid storage tank or a recreational vehicle, park trailer, or other similar vehicle, unless otherwise described. Cancellation. The ending of the insurance coverage provided by a policy before the expiration date. Condominium. That form of ownership of real property in which each unit owner has an undivided interest in common elements. Condominium Association. The entity made up of the unit owners responsible for the maintenance and operation of: Common elements owned in undivided shares by unit owners; and Other real property in which the unit owners have use rights; where membership in the entity is a required condition of unit ownership. Declarations Page. A computer-generated summary of information provided in the application for insurance. The Declarations Page describes the term of the policy, limits of coverage, and displays the premium and company name. The Declarations Page is a part of the flood insurance policy. Described Location. The location where the insured buildings or personal property are found. The "described location" is shown on the Declarations Page. Direct Physical Loss By or From Flood. Loss or damage to insured property, directly caused by a flood. There must be evidence of physical changes to the property. Dwelling. A building designed for use as a residence for no more than four families or a single-family unit in a building under a condominium form of ownership. Elevated Building. A building that has no basement and its lowest elevated floor raised above ground level by foundation walls, shear walls, posts, piers, pilings, or columns. Emergency Program. The initial phase of a community's participation in the National Flood Insurance Program. During this phase, only limited amounts of insurance are available under the Act. Enclosure. That portion of an elevated building below the lowest elevated floor that is partially or fully shut in by rigid walls. Expense Constant. A flat charge on each new or renewal policy to defray the expenses of the Federal Government related to flood insurance. Federal Policy Fee. A flat charge on each new or renewal policy to defray certain administrative expenses incurred in carrying out the National Flood Insurance Program. This fee covers expenses not covered by the expense constant. Flood Hazard Boundary Map (FHBM). Official map of a community issued by FEMA, where the boundaries of the flood, mudflow, and related erosion areas having special hazards have been designated. Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM). Official map of a community on which FEMA has delineated Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs), the Base Flood Elevations (BFEs), and risk premium zones applicable to the community. Grandfathering. A former NFIP rating procedure that is no longer available for policies written or renewed effective October 1, 2021, or later. Improvements. Fixtures, alterations, installations, or additions comprising a part of an insured dwelling or apartment. Lowest Floor. The lowest floor of the lowest enclosed area (including a basement). An unfinished or flood-resistant enclosure, usable solely for parking of vehicles, building access, or storage in an area other than a basement, is not considered a building's lowest floor provided such enclosure is not built so as to render the structure in violation of requirements. Lowest Floor Elevation (LFE). The measured distance of a building’s lowest floor above the National Geodetic Vertical Datum (NGVD) or other datum specified on the FIRM for that location. https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/Vertical_Datum_Conversion_Guidance_Nov_2023.pdf Mudflow. A river of liquid and flowing mud on the surfaces of normally dry land areas, as when earth is carried by a current of water. Other earth movements, such as landslide, slope failure, or a saturated soil mass moving by liquidity down a slope, are not mudflows. National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). The program of flood insurance coverage and floodplain management administered under the Act and applicable Federal regulations in Title 44 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Subchapter B. Policy. The entire written contract. It includes: The application and Declarations Page; Any endorsements issued; and Any renewal certificate indicating that coverage has been instituted for a new policy and new policy term. Only one dwelling, specifically described in the application, may be insured under a policy. Pollutants. Substances that include, but are not limited to, any solid, liquid, gaseous, or thermal irritant or contaminant, including smoke, vapor, soot, fumes, acids, alkalis, chemicals, and waste. "Waste" includes, but is not limited to, materials to be recycled, reconditioned, or reclaimed. Post-FIRM Building. A building for which construction or substantial improvement occurred after December 31, 1974, or on or after the effective date of an initial Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM), whichever is later. Pre-FIRM Building. A building for which construction or substantial improvement occurred on or before December 31, 1974, or before the effective date of an initial Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM). Probation Premium. A flat charge on each new or renewal policy issued covering property in a community that the NFIP has placed on probation under the provisions of 44 CFR 59.24. Regular Program. The final phase of a community's participation in the National Flood Insurance Program. In this phase, a Flood Insurance Rate Map is in effect and full limits of coverage are available under the Act. Replacement Cost Value (RCV). The amount of money required to replace or repair the insured building in the event of loss or damage, without a deduction for depreciation. Section 1316. Section of the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968, as amended, which states that no new flood insurance coverage can be provided for any property that FEMA finds has been declared by a duly constituted state or local zoning authority or other authorized public body to be in violation of state or local laws, regulations, or ordinances intended to discourage or otherwise restrict land development or occupancy in flood-prone areas. Severe Repetitive Loss Building. Any building that is covered under a Standard Flood Insurance Policy made available under this title, that has incurred flood damage for which: 4 or more separate claim payments have been made under a Standard Flood Insurance Policy issued pursuant to this title, with the amount of each such claim exceeding $5,000, and with the cumulative amount of such claims payments exceeding $20,000; or At least 2 separate claims payments have been made under a Standard Flood Insurance Policy, with the cumulative amount of such claim payments exceeding the fair market value of the insured building on the day before each loss. Severe Repetitive Loss (SRL) Properties. Either a severe repetitive loss building or the contents within a severe repetitive loss building, or both. Special Flood Hazard Area. An area having special flood, or mudflow, and/or flood-related erosion hazards, and shown on a Flood Hazard Boundary Map or Flood Insurance Rate Map as Zone be A, AO, AH, A1-30, AE, A99, AR, AR/A1-30, AR/AE, AR/AO, AR/AH, AR/A, VO, V1-30, VE, or V . Submit-for-Rate. An application for flood insurance on a building for which no risk rate is published in the NFIP Flood Insurance Manual. Insurance coverage can be obtained only after the NFIP has approved the application and has established the risk premium rate. Unit. A single-family unit in a condominium building. Valued Policy. A policy in which the insured and the insurer agree on the value of the property insured, that value being payable in the event of a total loss. The is not a valued policy. 4.6 Flood Policy Coverages The Standard Flood Insurance Policy provides four standard coverages: Coverage A - Building Property Coverage B - Personal Property Coverage C - Other Coverages Coverage D - Increased Cost of Compliance Standard Flood Policies are single-peril (flood) policies that pay for direct physical damage to insured property up to the replacement cost or Actual Cash Value (ACV) of the actual damages or the policy limit of liability, whichever is less. 4.7 Property Not Covered A flood policy does not cover: Personal property not inside the fully enclosed building; A building, and personal property in it, located entirely in, on, or over water or seaward of mean high tide if it was constructed or substantially improved after September 30, 1982; Open structures, including a building used as a boathouse or any structure or building into which boats are floated, and personal property located in, on, or over water; Recreational vehicles other than travel trailers described in II.B.6.c., whether affixed to a permanent foundation or on wheels; Self-propelled vehicles or machines, including their parts and equipment. However, we do cover self-propelled vehicles or machines not licensed for use on public roads that are: Used mainly to service the "described location," or Designed and used to assist handicapped persons, while the vehicles or machines are inside a building at the "described location;" Land, land values, lawns, trees, shrubs, plants, growing crops, or animals; Accounts, bills, coins, currency, deeds, evidences of debt, medals, money, scrip, stored value cards, postage stamps, securities, bullion, manuscripts, or other valuable papers; Underground structures and equipment, including wells, septic tanks, and septic systems; Those portions of walks, walkways, decks, driveways, patios, and other surfaces, all whether protected by a roof or not, located outside the perimeter, exterior walls of the insured building or the building in which the insured unit is located; Containers, including related equipment, such as, but not limited to, tanks containing gases or liquids; Buildings or units and all their contents if more than 49 percent of the actual cash value of the building or unit is below ground, unless the lowest level is at or above the BFE and is below ground by reason of earth having been used as insulation material in conjunction with energy efficient building techniques; Fences, retaining walls, seawalls, bulkheads, wharves, piers, bridges, and docks; Aircraft or watercraft, or their furnishings and equipment; Hot tubs and spas that are not bathroom fixtures, and swimming pools, and their equipment such as, but not limited to, heaters, filters, pumps, and pipes, wherever located; Property not eligible for flood insurance pursuant to the provisions of the Coastal Barrier Resources Act and the Coastal Barrier Improvement Act and amendments to these acts; Personal property owned in common with other unit owners comprising the membership of a condominium association. 4.8 Exclusions As you have learned, coverage under a flood policy only provides coverage for direct physical loss by or from a flood. Excluded from coverage: Loss of revenue or profits; Loss of access to the insured property or "described location;" Loss of use of the insured property or "described location"; Loss from interruption of business or production; Any additional living expenses incurred while the insured building is being repaired or is unable to be occupied for any reason; The cost of complying with any ordinance or law requiring or regulating the construction, demolition, remodeling, renovation, or repair of property, including removal of any resulting debris. This exclusion does not apply to any eligible activities that we describe in Coverage D - Increased Cost of Compliance; or Any other economic loss. Losses directly or indirectly caused by a flood that is already in progress at the time and date: The policy term begins; or Coverage is added at request of the insured. Loss to property caused directly by earth movement even if the earth movement is caused by flood. Examples include: Earthquake; Landslide; Land subsidence; Sinkholes; Destabilization or movement of land that results from accumulation of water in subsurface land area; or Gradual erosion. Key Point: Coverage is available for losses from mudflow and any land subsidence as a result of erosion covered under the standard definition of flood. Direct physical loss caused directly or indirectly by any of the following: The pressure or weight of ice; Freezing or thawing; Rain, snow, sleet, hail, or water spray; Water, moisture, mildew, or mold damage that results primarily from any condition: Substantially confined to the dwelling; or That is within the insured's control, including but not limited to: Design, structural, or mechanical defects; Failure, stoppage, or breakage of water or sewer lines, drains, pumps, fixtures, or equipment; or Failure to inspect and maintain the property after a flood recedes; Water or waterborne material that: Backs up through sewers or drains; Discharges or overflows from a sump, sump pump, or related equipment; or Seeps or leaks on or through the covered property; unless there is a flood in the area and the flood is the proximate cause of the sewer or drain backup, sump pump discharge or overflow, or seepage of water; The pressure or weight of water unless there is a flood in the area and the flood is the proximate cause of the damage from the pressure or weight of water; Power, heating, or cooling failure unless the failure results from direct physical loss by or from flood to power, heating, or cooling equipment on the "described location;" Theft, fire, explosion, wind, or windstorm; Anything the insured or any member of the insured's household do or conspire to do to cause loss by flood deliberately; or Alteration of the insured property that significantly increases the risk of flooding. Loss to any building or personal property located on land leased from the Federal Government, arising from or incident to the flooding of the land by the Federal Government, where the lease expressly holds the Federal Government harmless under flood insurance issued under any Federal Government program. Testing for or monitoring of pollutants unless required by law or ordinance. Knowledge Check Which of the following is the cost to replace an insured item of property at the time of loss minus the value of its physical depreciation? Actual cash value is defined as the cost to replace an insured item of property at the time of loss, less the value of its physical depreciation.] Actual replacement cost [Your answer is incorrect. In most cases, a higher deductible may reduce the premium. Contents-only policies (policies with no building coverage) receive a minimum $1,000 deductible. Policyholders can select any combination of building and contents deductibles for Single-Family Home, Residential Manufactured/Mobile Home, Residential Unit, and Two-to-Four Family Building occupancies. For all other building occupancies, the NFIP offers building and contents deductible options in fixed combinations. Deductible Increases: Policyholders may increase deductibles during the current policy term. The earliest effective date of the increased deductible is the date the insurer receives the endorsement request. However, if a policyholder with a provisionally rated policy and standard $2,000 deductible selects a higher deductible when transitioning to a rating engine rate, use the effective date of the current policy term. Deductible Decreases: Insurers may decrease deductibles during the current policy term only in the following instances: • If the property has a mortgage and the mortgagee requires a lower deductible • If a policyholder with a provisionally rated policy and standard $2,000 deductible selects a lower deductible when transitioning to a rating engine rate. 5.2 Loss Settlement A flood policy provides three methods of settling losses: Replacement Cost, Special Loss Settlement, and Actual Cash Value. Replacement Cost loss settlement applies to a single-family dwelling, provided: It is your principal residence, which means that, at the time of loss, you or your spouse lived there for at least 80 percent of: The 365 days immediately preceding the loss; or (b) The period of your ownership, if you owned the dwelling for less than 365 days; and (2) At the time of loss, the amount of insurance in this policy that applies to the dwelling is 80 percent or more of its full replacement cost immediately before the loss, or is the maximum amount of insurance available under the NFIP. The replacement cost loss settlement provisions provide: We will pay to repair or replace the damaged dwelling after application of the deductible and without deduction for depreciation, but not more than the least of the following amounts: The building limit of liability shown on your Declarations Page; The replacement cost of that part of the dwelling damaged, with materials of like kind and quality, and for like use; or (3) The necessary amount actually spent to repair or replace the damaged part of the dwelling for like use. If the dwelling is rebuilt at a new location, the cost described above is limited to the cost that would have been incurred if the dwelling had been rebuilt at its former location. When the full cost of repair or replacement is more than $1,000 or more than 5 percent of the whole amount of insurance that applies to the dwelling, we will not be liable for any loss under V.2.a. above or V.4.a.(2) below unless and until actual repair or replacement is completed. You may disregard the replacement cost conditions above and make claim under this policy for loss to dwellings on an actual cash value basis. You may then make claim for any additional liability according to V.2.a., b., and c. above, provided you notify us of your intent to do so within 180 days after the date of loss. If the community in which your dwelling is located has been converted from the Emergency Program to the Regular Program during the current policy term, then we will consider the maximum amount of available NFIP insurance to be the amount that was available at the beginning of the current policy term. Special loss settlement applies to a single-family dwelling that is a manufactured or mobile home or a travel trailer. The following loss settlement conditions apply to single-family dwellings: Is a manufactured or mobile home or a travel trailer, as defined in II.B.6.b. and II.B.6.c.; Is at least 16 feet wide when fully assembled and has an area of at least 600 square feet within its perimeter walls when fully assembled; and (3) Is your principal residence, as specified in V.1.a.(1) above. If such a dwelling is totally destroyed or damaged to such an extent that, in our judgment, it is not economically feasible to repair, at least to its pre-damage condition, we will, at our discretion, pay the least of the following amounts: The lesser of the replacement cost of the dwelling or 1.5 times the actual cash value, or The building limit of liability shown on your Declarations Page. If such a dwelling is partially damaged and, in our judgment, it is economically feasible to repair it to its pre-damage condition, we will settle the loss according to the Replacement Cost conditions in paragraph V.2. above. Actual Cash Value loss settlement applies to a single-family dwelling not subject to replacement cost or special loss settlement, and to the following properties: A dwelling, at the time of loss, when the amount of insurance on the dwelling is both less than 80 percent of its full replacement cost immediately before the loss and less than the maximum amount of insurance available under the NFIP. In that case, we will pay the greater of the following amounts, but not more than the amount of insurance that applies to that dwelling: The actual cash value of the damaged part of the dwelling; or A proportion of the cost to repair or replace the damaged part of the dwelling, without deduction for physical depreciation and after application of the deductible. This proportion is determined as follows: If 80 percent of the full replacement cost of the dwelling is less than the maximum amount of insurance available under the NFIP, then the proportion is determined by dividing the actual amount of insurance on the dwelling by the amount of insurance that represents 80 percent of its full replacement cost. But if 80 percent of the full replacement cost of the dwelling is greater than the maximum amount of insurance available under the NFIP, then the proportion is determined by dividing the actual amount of insurance on the dwelling by the maximum amount of insurance available under the NFIP. A two-, three-, or four-family dwelling A unit that is not used exclusively for single-family dwelling purposes; Detached garages; Personal property; Appliances, carpets, and carpet pads; Outdoor awnings, outdoor antennas or aerials of any type, and other outdoor equipment Any property covered under this policy that is abandoned after a loss and remains as debris anywhere on the "described location;" A dwelling that is not your principal residence. 5.2.1 Coinsurance Penalty in RCBAP The RCBAP’s coinsurance penalty is applied to building coverage only. To the extent that the insured has not purchased insurance in an amount equal to the lesser of 80 percent or more of the full replacement cost of the building at the time of loss or the maximum amount of insurance under the NFIP, the insured will not be fully reimbursed for a loss. Building coverage purchased under individual Dwelling Forms cannot be added to RCBAP coverage in order to avoid the coinsurance penalty. The amount of loss in this case will be determined by using the following formula: Insurance Carried X Amount of Loss = Limit of Recovery Insurance Required. Where the penalty applies, building loss under the RCBAP will be adjusted based on the Replacement Cost Coverage with a coinsurance penalty. Building loss under the Dwelling Form will be adjusted on an Actual Cash Value (ACV) basis if the Replacement Cost provision is not met. The cost of bringing the building into compliance with local codes (law and ordinance) is not included in the calculation of replacement cost. 5.3 Reduction and Reformation of Coverage The Reduction and Reformation of Coverage section of a flood policy states that if premiums received from the insured are not enough to buy the type and amount of requested coverage, the insurer will only provide the amount of coverage the premium received will cover. If the policy coverage is reduced due to insufficient premium payment, the policy may be reformed under the following circumstances: If the insufficient premium or incomplete rating information is discovered before a loss, the insurer will send the insured, and any mortgagee or trustee known to the insurer, a bill for the required additional premium for the current policy term (or that portion of the current policy term following any endorsement changing the amount of coverage). If that additional premium is paid within 30 days from the date of the bill, the policy will be reformed to increase the amount of coverage to the originally requested amount effective to the beginning of the current policy term (or subsequent date of any endorsement changing the amount of coverage). Additionally, if the insurer determines before the insured has a flood loss that the rating information is incomplete and prevents the insurer from calculating the additional premium, the required information will be requested from the insured. The insured must then submit the required information within 60 days of request. Finally, if the insurer does not receive the additional premium (or additional information) by the date it is due, the amount of coverage can only be increased by endorsement subject to any appropriate waiting period. If the insufficient premium or incomplete rating information is discovered after a loss, the insurer will send the insured, and any mortgagee or trustee known to the insured, a bill for the required additional premium for the current and the prior policy terms. If the insured or the mortgagee or trustee pay the additional premium within 30 days from the date of the bill, the policy will be reformed to increase the amount of coverage to the originally requested amount effective to the beginning of the prior policy term. Additionally, if the insurer discovers after a flood loss that the rating information they possess is incomplete and prevents them from calculating the additional premium, the insurer will request the information required to complete the calculation. The information must be submitted before the claim can be paid. Finally, if the insurer does not receive the additional premium by the date it is due, the flood insurance claim will be settled based on the reduced amount of coverage. The amount of coverage can only be increased by endorsement subject to any appropriate waiting period. Importantly, if the insurer determines the insured or their agent intentionally did not tell them, or falsified, any important fact or circumstance or did anything fraudulent relating to the insurance, the policy: is void as of the date the wrongful acts were committed; has no legal force or effect; cannot be renewed; and cannot be replaced by a new NFIP policy. Fines, civil penalties, and imprisonment under applicable federal laws may also apply to the acts of fraud or concealment. There are reasons other than fraud, misrepresentation, or wrongful acts that a policy may be void. These include: if the property is located in a community that was not participating in the NFIP on the policy's inception date and did not join or reenter the program during the policy term and before the loss occurred; or if the property listed on the application is otherwise not eligible for coverage under the NFIP. 5.4 Waiting Period There is a standard 30-day waiting period for new applications and for endorsements to increase coverage. This waiting period is calculated as follows: If the application or endorsement form and the premium payment are received at the NFIP within 10 days from the date of application or endorsement request, or if mailed by certified mail within 4 days from the date of application or endorsement request, then the waiting period will be calculated from the application or endorsement date. Use the application date or endorsement date plus 9 days to determine if the application or endorsement and premium payment were received within 10 days. When sent by certified mail, use the application date or endorsement date plus 3 days to determine if the application or endorsement and premium payment were mailed within 4 days. If the application or endorsement form and the premium payment are received at the NFIP after 10 days from the date of application or endorsement request, or are not mailed by certified mail within 4 days from the date of application or endorsement request, then the waiting period will be calculated from the date the NFIP receives the application or endorsement. 5.5 Policy Term The policy term is one year for NFIP policies and those written through WYO companies. There is a standard 30-day waiting period before a policy can take effect. response: Flood Insurance Basics introduces insurance professionals and other property-related practitioners to the National Flood Insurance Program and the practical rules that govern flood coverage. The course emphasizes why this topic matters: flooding can occur in many settings, standard homeowners insurance generally excludes flood loss, and lenders and consumers rely on accurate guidance about when coverage is required or advisable. The material moves from NFIP foundations, community participation, and property eligibility to flood maps, zones, and map changes that affect underwriting and purchase requirements. It then explains available policy forms, covered and excluded property, core policy provisions, rating steps, and the claims process, including insured and producer responsibilities. Learners finish better prepared to identify eligible risks, explain coverage options, apply NFIP rules, support claims handling, and meet agent duties when advising consumers.

1.0 Anywhere There Is Water

Flooding can occur anywhere there is water.

Flooding is defined as:

A general and temporary condition of partial or complete inundation of two or more acres of normally dry land area or of two or more properties (at least one of which is the policyholder’s property) from:

overflow of inland or tidal waters;

unusual and rapid accumulation or runoff of surface waters from any source; or – mudflow; or

collapse or subsidence of land along the shore of a lake or similar body of water as a result of erosion or undermining caused by waves or currents of water exceeding anticipated cyclical levels that result in a flood.

The most common events that result in flooding include hurricanes, broken levees, outdated or clogged drainage systems, or a heavy rainfall. Risk of flooding is based on a number of factors, including:

history,

rainfall,

river-flow and tidal surge data,

topography,

flood-control measures, and

changes due to building and development.

Unfortunately, it takes little water to do major damage and a typical homeowners policy does not include coverage for flooding, making flood insurance a necessity for those at increased risk for flooding.   Congress requires that federally regulated or insured lenders require flood insurance on properties that are located in areas at high risk of flooding.  High risk areas have a 1% or greater chance of flooding in any given year, which is equivalent to a 26% chance of flooding during a 30-year mortgage.  Although homes and businesses located in moderate-to-low risk areas are typically not required to have flood insurance, it is highly recommended because they too can be financially vulnerable to floods.

This course will discuss the National Flood Insurance Program and the coverage options available to address potential flood hazards.

Learning Objectives

After you have completed this course, you will be able to . . .

Describe the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), identify the types of buildings and other property that can get coverage under this program, and identify who needs flood insurance;

Explain the function of flood maps and flood zones under the NFIP;

Discuss the types of policies under the NFIP, including dwelling policies, general property policies, and residential condominium policies, and explain their uses;

Explain the general rules governing policies, including deductibles, waiting periods, cancellations, etc.;

Describe the rating steps that must be followed to set a premium for an NFIP policy;

Discuss the way in which claims are handled, including responsibilities of the insured; and

Describe an agent’s responsibilities is selling NFIP insurance to consumers.

The NFIP is administered by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the information contained in this course relies heavily on the FEMA Flood Insurance Manual. FEMA updates this manual a couple times a year; you can access the current and past manuals here.

2.0 The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) Background

In 1968, Congress established the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) to:

Authorize a flood insurance program that, over time, could be made available on a nationwide basis through the cooperative effort of the federal government and the private insurance industry.

Provide flexibility in the program so that such flood insurance would be based on workable methods of pooling risks, minimizing costs and distributing burdens equitably among the general public and those who would be protected by flood insurance.

Encourage state and local governments to use wisely the lands under their jurisdictions by considering the hazards of flood when rendering decisions on the future use of such land in order to minimize damage.

In 1983, the Write Your Own (WYO) Program was established through a joint effort of FEMA and the private insurance industry. According to FEMA:

The WYO Program allows participating property and casualty insurance companies to write and service the Standard Flood Insurance Policy in their own names. The companies receive an expense allowance for policies written and claims processed while the Federal Government retains responsibility for underwriting losses. The WYO Program operates as part of the NFIP, and is subject to its rules and regulations.

Under the NFIP program, communities agree, through adoption of codes and ordinances, to regulate the use of flood-prone land. In exchange, FEMA makes flood insurance coverage available on buildings and their contents throughout the community. To assist communities with identifying these flood-prone areas, FEMA has created flood hazard maps. In addition to assisting communities, the flood hazard maps assist insurance producers in setting rates and lenders with regard to purchase requirements.

The Coastal Barrier Resources Act (CBRA), and the Coastal Barrier Improvement Act (CBIA) of 1990, were implemented to:

minimize loss of life by discouraging development in high-risk areas,

reduce wasteful expenditures of federal resources, and

preserve the ecological integrity of areas Congress designates as a Coastal Barrier Resources System (CBRS) and Otherwise Protected Areas (OPAs),

by prohibiting federal expenditures or financial assistance (including flood insurance) for residential or commercial development in areas identified as high risk.

FEMA provides a list of communities where coastal barriers or OPAs are identified and should be consulted prior to insuring a property. You may view the complete list in the Flood Insurance Manual.

3.1 Types of Flood Maps

There are two types of maps used for rating flood insurance:

the Flood Hazard Boundary Map (FHBM) and

the Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM).

The FHBM is issued by FEMA and represents the official map of a community, showing where the boundaries of the flood, mudflow, and related erosion areas having special hazards have been designated.

A FIRM is the official map of a community on which FEMA has delineated the special hazard areas and the risk premium zones applicable to the community. The FIRM is typically used for Regular Program communities.

Key Point:

An FHBM is the initial flood hazard identification map, typically used in Emergency Program communities.

There are times when Regular Program communities will use a map that was originally published as an FHBM. When this occurs, a letter accompanies the map outlining conversion to the Regular Program and indicating that the FHBM map should now be considered a FIRM.

3.2 Changing or Correcting a Flood Map

There are times when a change to a flood map is required and the NFIP has certain procedures that must be followed to facilitate such amendments. The Flood Manual outlines these procedures as:

Letter of Map Amendment (LOMA). A LOMA is used in instances where an applicant/insured believes they are being required to purchase flood insurance in error and that their property is not actually located in the SFHA. The insured then requests a LOMA asking FEMA to make a correction.

Letter of Map Revision (LOMR). A LOMR is an official revision to a current FEMA map. A LOMR must be requested directly from the CEO of a community, as any changes made because of the LOMR must be adopted by the community.

Physical Map Revision. A physical map revision is exactly what it sounds like: change and republication of an existing map to change flood insurance zones, floodplain delineations, flood elevations, floodways, and planimetric features.

Letter of Map Amendment (LOMA). A LOMA is used in instances where an applicant/insured believes they are being required to purchase flood insurance in error and that their property is not actually located in the SFHA. The insured then requests a LOMA asking FEMA to make a correction.

4.4 Preferred Risk Policy (PRP)

We are going to briefly mention a policy type that was recently eliminated. It was the Preferred Risk Policy (PRP), which offered low-cost coverage to owners and tenants of properties located in zones B, C, and X in eligible Regular Program communities. 

Although this form was eliminated as a separate policy-type as of October 1, 2021, the low-cost coverage offered under the form was incorporated into the Dwelling Policy.

Key Point:

For residential properties, the maximum coverage combination is $250,000: building and $100,000 contents. Up to $100,000 contents-only coverage is available. For non-residential properties, the maximum coverage combination is $500,000 building and $500,000 contents. Up to $500,000 contents-only coverage is available. Only one building can be insured per policy, and only one policy can be written on each building.

Coverage previously available under the PRP that may be gotten now under the Dwelling Policy includes:

Combined building/contents insurance, available for owners of all eligible occupancy types—one- to four-family properties (including individual condominium units in condominium buildings), other residential properties, and non-residential properties.

Contents-only coverage, available for tenants and owners of all eligible occupancies, unless the contents are located entirely in a basement.

Eligibility for the PRP was also based on a building’s flood loss history, meaning if one of the following conditions existed within any 10-year period (regardless of any change(s) in ownership of the building), the building was not eligible for the PRP:

Two flood insurance claim payments, each more than $1,000; or

Three or more flood insurance claim payments, regardless of amount; or

Two federal flood disaster relief payments (including loans and grants), each more than $1,000; or

Three federal flood disaster relief payments (including loans and grants), regardless of amount; or

One flood insurance claim payment and one federal flood disaster relief payment (including loans and grants), each more than $1,000.

4.5 Flood Policy Definitions

Act. The National Flood Insurance Act of 1968 and any amendments to it.

Actual Cash Value (ACV). The cost to replace an insured item of property at the time of loss, less the value of its physical depreciation.

Application. The statement made and signed by the customer or agent in applying for the policy. The application provides information used to determine the eligibility of the risk, the kind of policy to be issued, and the correct premium payment. The application is part of the flood insurance policy. The correct premium payment must accompany the application.

Base Flood. A flood having a one percent chance of being equaled or exceeded in any given year.

Basement. Any area of the building, including any sunken room or sunken portion of a room, having its floor below ground level (subgrade) on all sides.

Binder or Certificate of Insurance. A temporary agreement between company, producer, and insured that the policy is in effect. The NFIP does not recognize binders. However, the NFIP recognizes Certificates of Insurance for renewal policies.

Blanket Insurance. A single amount of insurance applying to more than one building and/or contents. Blanket insurance is not permitted under the NFIP.

Building. A building is defined in the program as:

A structure with two or more outside rigid walls and a fully secured roof, that is affixed to a permanent site;

A manufactured home (a "manufactured home," also known as a mobile home, is a structure: built on a permanent chassis, transported to its site in one or more sections, and affixed to a permanent foundation); or

A travel trailer without wheels, built on a chassis and affixed to a permanent foundation, that is regulated under the community's floodplain management and building ordinances or laws.

This definition does not include a gas or liquid storage tank or a recreational vehicle, park trailer, or other similar vehicle, unless otherwise described.

Cancellation. The ending of the insurance coverage provided by a policy before the expiration date.

Condominium. That form of ownership of real property in which each unit owner has an undivided interest in common elements.

Condominium Association. The entity made up of the unit owners responsible for the maintenance and operation of:

Common elements owned in undivided shares by unit owners; and

Other real property in which the unit owners have use rights;

where membership in the entity is a required condition of unit ownership.

Declarations Page. A computer-generated summary of information provided in the application for insurance. The Declarations Page describes the term of the policy, limits of coverage, and displays the premium and company name. The Declarations Page is a part of the flood insurance policy.

Described Location. The location where the insured buildings or personal property are found. The "described location" is shown on the Declarations Page.

Direct Physical Loss By or From Flood. Loss or damage to insured property, directly caused by a flood. There must be evidence of physical changes to the property.

Dwelling. A building designed for use as a residence for no more than four families or a single-family unit in a building under a condominium form of ownership.

Elevated Building. A building that has no basement and its lowest elevated floor raised above ground level by foundation walls, shear walls, posts, piers, pilings, or columns.

Emergency Program. The initial phase of a community's participation in the National Flood Insurance Program. During this phase, only limited amounts of insurance are available under the Act.

Enclosure. That portion of an elevated building below the lowest elevated floor that is partially or fully shut in by rigid walls.

Expense Constant. A flat charge on each new or renewal policy to defray the expenses of the Federal Government related to flood insurance.

Federal Policy Fee. A flat charge on each new or renewal policy to defray certain administrative expenses incurred in carrying out the National Flood Insurance Program. This fee covers expenses not covered by the expense constant.

Flood Hazard Boundary Map (FHBM). Official map of a community issued by FEMA, where the boundaries of the flood, mudflow, and related erosion areas having special hazards have been designated.

Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM). Official map of a community on which FEMA has delineated Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs), the Base Flood Elevations (BFEs), and risk premium zones applicable to the community.

Grandfathering. A former NFIP rating procedure that is no longer available for policies written or renewed effective October 1, 2021, or later.

Improvements. Fixtures, alterations, installations, or additions comprising a part of an insured dwelling or apartment.

Lowest Floor. The lowest floor of the lowest enclosed area (including a basement). An unfinished or flood-resistant enclosure, usable solely for parking of vehicles, building access, or storage in an area other than a basement, is not considered a building's lowest floor provided such enclosure is not built so as to render the structure in violation of requirements.

Lowest Floor Elevation (LFE). The measured distance of a building’s lowest floor above the National Geodetic Vertical Datum (NGVD) or other datum specified on the FIRM for that location.

https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/Vertical_Datum_Conversion_Guidance_Nov_2023.pdf

Mudflow. A river of liquid and flowing mud on the surfaces of normally dry land areas, as when earth is carried by a current of water. Other earth movements, such as landslide, slope failure, or a saturated soil mass moving by liquidity down a slope, are not mudflows.

National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). The program of flood insurance coverage and floodplain management administered under the Act and applicable Federal regulations in Title 44 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Subchapter B.

Policy. The entire written contract. It includes:

The application and Declarations Page;

Any endorsements issued; and

Any renewal certificate indicating that coverage has been instituted for a new policy and new policy term.

Only one dwelling, specifically described in the application, may be insured under a policy.

Pollutants. Substances that include, but are not limited to, any solid, liquid, gaseous, or thermal irritant or contaminant, including smoke, vapor, soot, fumes, acids, alkalis, chemicals, and waste. "Waste" includes, but is not limited to, materials to be recycled, reconditioned, or reclaimed.

Post-FIRM Building. A building for which construction or substantial improvement occurred after December 31, 1974, or on or after the effective date of an initial Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM), whichever is later.

Pre-FIRM Building. A building for which construction or substantial improvement occurred on or before December 31, 1974, or before the effective date of an initial Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM).

Probation Premium. A flat charge on each new or renewal policy issued covering property in a community that the NFIP has placed on probation under the provisions of 44 CFR 59.24.

Regular Program. The final phase of a community's participation in the National Flood Insurance Program. In this phase, a Flood Insurance Rate Map is in effect and full limits of coverage are available under the Act.

Replacement Cost Value (RCV). The amount of money required to replace or repair the insured building in the event of loss or damage, without a deduction for depreciation.

Section 1316. Section of the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968, as amended, which states that no new flood insurance coverage can be provided for any property that FEMA finds has been declared by a duly constituted state or local zoning authority or other authorized public body to be in violation of state or local laws, regulations, or ordinances intended to discourage or otherwise restrict land development or occupancy in flood-prone areas.

Severe Repetitive Loss Building. Any building that is covered under a Standard Flood Insurance Policy made available under this title, that has incurred flood damage for which:

4 or more separate claim payments have been made under a Standard Flood Insurance Policy issued pursuant to this title, with the amount of each such claim exceeding $5,000, and with the cumulative amount of such claims payments exceeding $20,000; or

At least 2 separate claims payments have been made under a Standard Flood Insurance Policy, with the cumulative amount of such claim payments exceeding the fair market value of the insured building on the day before each loss.

Severe Repetitive Loss (SRL) Properties. Either a severe repetitive loss building or the contents within a severe repetitive loss building, or both.

Special Flood Hazard Area. An area having special flood, or mudflow, and/or flood-related erosion hazards, and shown on a Flood Hazard Boundary Map or Flood Insurance Rate Map as Zone be A, AO, AH, A1-30, AE, A99, AR, AR/A1-30, AR/AE, AR/AO, AR/AH, AR/A, VO, V1-30, VE, or V .

Submit-for-Rate. An application for flood insurance on a building for which no risk rate is published in the NFIP Flood Insurance Manual. Insurance coverage can be obtained only after the NFIP has approved the application and has established the risk premium rate.

Unit. A single-family unit in a condominium building.

Valued Policy. A policy in which the insured and the insurer agree on the value of the property insured, that value being payable in the event of a total loss. The is not a valued policy.

The Standard Flood Insurance Policy provides four standard coverages:

Coverage A - Building Property

4.7 Property Not Covered

A flood policy does not cover:

Personal property not inside the fully enclosed building;

A building, and personal property in it, located entirely in, on, or over water or seaward of mean high tide if it was constructed or substantially improved after September 30, 1982;

Open structures, including a building used as a boathouse or any structure or building into which boats are floated, and personal property located in, on, or over water;

Recreational vehicles other than travel trailers described in II.B.6.c., whether affixed to a permanent foundation or on wheels;

Self-propelled vehicles or machines, including their parts and equipment. However, we do cover self-propelled vehicles or machines not licensed for use on public roads that are:

Used mainly to service the "described location," or

Designed and used to assist handicapped persons, while the vehicles or machines are inside a building at the "described location;"

Land, land values, lawns, trees, shrubs, plants, growing crops, or animals;

Accounts, bills, coins, currency, deeds, evidences of debt, medals, money, scrip, stored value cards, postage stamps, securities, bullion, manuscripts, or other valuable papers;

Underground structures and equipment, including wells, septic tanks, and septic systems;

Those portions of walks, walkways, decks, driveways, patios, and other surfaces, all whether protected by a roof or not, located outside the perimeter, exterior walls of the insured building or the building in which the insured unit is located;

Containers, including related equipment, such as, but not limited to, tanks containing gases or liquids;

Buildings or units and all their contents if more than 49 percent of the actual cash value of the building or unit is below ground, unless the lowest level is at or above the BFE and is below ground by reason of earth having been used as insulation material in conjunction with energy efficient building techniques;

Fences, retaining walls, seawalls, bulkheads, wharves, piers, bridges, and docks;

Aircraft or watercraft, or their furnishings and equipment;

Hot tubs and spas that are not bathroom fixtures, and swimming pools, and their equipment such as, but not limited to, heaters, filters, pumps, and pipes, wherever located;

Property not eligible for flood insurance pursuant to the provisions of the Coastal Barrier Resources Act and the Coastal Barrier Improvement Act and amendments to these acts;

Personal property owned in common with other unit owners comprising the membership of a condominium association.

4.8 Exclusions

As you have learned, coverage under a flood policy only provides coverage for direct physical loss by or from a flood. Excluded from coverage:

Loss of revenue or profits;

Loss of access to the insured property or "described location;"

Loss of use of the insured property or "described location";

Loss from interruption of business or production;

Any additional living expenses incurred while the insured building is being repaired or is unable to be occupied for any reason;

The cost of complying with any ordinance or law requiring or regulating the construction, demolition, remodeling, renovation, or repair of property, including removal of any resulting debris. This exclusion does not apply to any eligible activities that we describe in Coverage D - Increased Cost of Compliance; or

Any other economic loss.

Losses directly or indirectly caused by a flood that is already in progress at the time and date:

The policy term begins; or

Coverage is added at request of the insured.

Loss to property caused directly by earth movement even if the earth movement is caused by flood. Examples include:

Earthquake;

Landslide;

Land subsidence;

Sinkholes;

Destabilization or movement of land that results from accumulation of water in subsurface land area; or

Gradual erosion.

Key Point:

Coverage is available for losses from mudflow and any land subsidence as a result of erosion covered under the standard definition of flood.

Direct physical loss caused directly or indirectly by any of the following:

The pressure or weight of ice;

Freezing or thawing;

Rain, snow, sleet, hail, or water spray;

Water, moisture, mildew, or mold damage that results primarily from any condition:

Substantially confined to the dwelling; or

That is within the insured's control, including but not limited to:

Design, structural, or mechanical defects;

Failure, stoppage, or breakage of water or sewer lines, drains, pumps, fixtures, or equipment; or

Failure to inspect and maintain the property after a flood recedes;

Water or waterborne material that:

Backs up through sewers or drains;

Discharges or overflows from a sump, sump pump, or related equipment; or

Seeps or leaks on or through the covered property;

unless there is a flood in the area and the flood is the proximate cause of the sewer or drain backup, sump pump discharge or overflow, or seepage of water;

The pressure or weight of water unless there is a flood in the area and the flood is the proximate cause of the damage from the pressure or weight of water;

Power, heating, or cooling failure unless the failure results from direct physical loss by or from flood to power, heating, or cooling equipment on the "described location;"

Theft, fire, explosion, wind, or windstorm;

Anything the insured or any member of the insured's household do or conspire to do to cause loss by flood deliberately; or

Alteration of the insured property that significantly increases the risk of flooding.

Loss to any building or personal property located on land leased from the Federal Government, arising from or incident to the flooding of the land by the Federal Government, where the lease expressly holds the Federal Government harmless under flood insurance issued under any Federal Government program.

Testing for or monitoring of pollutants unless required by law or ordinance.

Knowledge Check

Which of the following is the cost to replace an insured item of property at the time of loss minus the value of its physical depreciation? (Refer to Section 4.5, page 9)

Replacement cost value [Your answer is incorrect. Actual cash value is defined as the cost to replace an insured item of property at the time of loss, less the value of its physical depreciation.]

Depreciated replacement cost [Your answer is incorrect. Actual cash value is defined as the cost to replace an insured item of property at the time of loss, less the value of its physical depreciation.]

Actual cash value [Your answer is correct. Actual cash value is defined as the cost to replace an insured item of property at the time of loss, less the value of its physical depreciation.]

Actual replacement cost [Your answer is incorrect. Actual cash value is defined as the cost to replace an insured item of property at the time of loss, less the value of its physical depreciation.]

What type of policy would the resident of a condominium use for flood protection of their unit and its contents? (Refer to Section 4.3, page 8)

Dwelling Policy [Your answer is correct. The condo association uses the RCBAP and the unit owner uses the Dwelling Policy.]

General Property Policy [Your answer is incorrect. The condo association uses the RCBAP and the unit owner uses the Dwelling Policy. The General Property Policy is generally used for larger apartments and non-residential buildings.]

Preferred Risk Policy (PRP) [Your answer is incorrect. The condo association uses the RCBAP and the unit owner uses the Dwelling Policy.  The PRP no longer exists, but its coverage can be obtained under the Dwelling Policy.]

Residential Condominium Building Association Policy (RCBAP) [Your answer is incorrect. The condo association uses the RCBAP and the unit owner uses the Dwelling Policy.]

Which of the following is covered under the Standard Flood Insurance Policy? (Refer to Section 4.7, page 13)

Personal property not inside the fully enclosed building [Your answer is incorrect. Damage to the insured building is covered; the other items are not.]

Lawns, trees, shrubs, or other plants growing on the property [Your answer is incorrect. Damage to the insured building is covered; the other items are not.]

Damage to the insured building [Your answer is correct. Damage to the insured building is covered; the other items are not.]

Fences, retaining walls, seawalls, bulkheads, wharves, piers, bridges, or docks [Your answer is incorrect. Damage to the insured building is covered; the other items are not.]

5.1 Deductibles

The minimum deductible for building coverage varies based on the building occupancy, Pre-FIRM or Post-FIRM construction, receipt of statutory discounts, and the amount of building coverage purchased. In most cases, a higher deductible may reduce the premium. Contents-only policies (policies with no building coverage) receive a minimum $1,000 deductible.

Policyholders can select any combination of building and contents deductibles for Single-Family Home, Residential Manufactured/Mobile Home, Residential Unit, and Two-to-Four Family Building occupancies. For all other building occupancies, the NFIP offers building and contents deductible options in fixed combinations.

Deductible Increases: Policyholders may increase deductibles during the current policy term. The earliest effective date of the increased deductible is the date the insurer receives the endorsement request. However, if a policyholder with a provisionally rated policy and standard $2,000 deductible selects a higher deductible when transitioning to a rating engine rate, use the effective date of the current policy term.

Deductible Decreases: Insurers may decrease deductibles during the current policy term only in the following instances:

• If the property has a mortgage and the mortgagee requires a lower deductible

• If a policyholder with a provisionally rated policy and standard $2,000 deductible selects a lower deductible when transitioning to a rating engine rate.
